NeurIPS 2026 Workshop

When Feedback Becomes a Backdoor: Tracing Backdoor Skill Formation in Text-Space Skill Optimization

Louise Nayeong Koh1*† Yaechan Lee2* Myeongjong Lee3* Doyeon Kim4
Juyoung Park5 Seunggyu Kim4 Inseo Kim6 Chaerin Jung5 Hyogon Ryu7†
1Yonsei University 2Inha University 3Konkuk University 4Sungkyunkwan University
5Ewha Womans University 6Konyang University 7KRAFTON
Abstract

Reference answers are a supervision channel in text-space Skill optimization, which produces reusable text artifacts called Skills that guide future agent behavior. Poisoning those answers can induce a persistent trigger-conditioned rule without giving the attacker access to the model, optimizer, or Skill file. We study this reference-feedback poisoning in SkillOpt by tracing an attacker-supplied trigger–payload mapping from reflection to held-out activation. In SearchQA, where the payload replaces a short answer, the natural attack retains an exact rule in all three seeds; each final Skill emits the payload on 200/200 triggered questions and 0/200 clean questions. In seed 42, removing the rule eliminates activation, and an in-run comparison shows similar clean accuracy to benign SkillOpt (169/200 versus 171/200). In SpreadsheetBench, where the payload requires an additional workbook edit, no natural run retains an exact rule across three seeds. Diagnostic interventions locate two successive bottlenecks: the Analyst abstracts away required literals, and, once literal preservation is enabled, edit-budget ranking can remove exact edits before candidate construction. Poisoned references can therefore create persistent backdoors, but exposure alone does not ensure that the induced rule is formed, selected, and retained.

**footnotetext: Equal contribution.††footnotetext: Correspondence to Louise Nayeong Koh (louisenyk@yonsei.ac.kr) and Hyogon Ryu (hyogon.ryu@gmail.com).

1 Introduction

Self-evolving agents improve by converting execution experience into persistent natural-language Skills. A text-space skill optimizer, such as SkillOpt [1], runs the target model on a batch of tasks, scores the outputs against reference answers, reflects on failures, proposes textual edits, and retains a candidate Skill if it achieves a higher score on a validation set. The resulting Skill is reused on every later task. Supervision provided during optimization can therefore shape behavior well beyond the examples it came from.

Prior work has shown that this persistent state can be manipulated through memory and retrieval stores [7, 8], poisoned experience [5], malicious queries and trajectories [2, 3, 4], and directly supplied Skill files [6]. Poisoned human feedback has also been used to implant backdoors during weight-space RLHF [10]. Here we study a different feedback channel: reference answers used to judge an agent’s executions during text-space Skill optimization. A poisoned training reference changes which executions are labeled as failures and thus what the optimizer reflects on. A poisoned validation reference changes which candidate wins. When optimization tasks draw on contributed or externally maintained datasets, the provenance and integrity of their reference answers can be difficult to verify.

Exposure is not persistence. A trigger–payload rule must be recognized, written as an executable edit, survive merging and ranking, enter a candidate, pass validation, remain in the endpoint Skill, and activate on held-out inputs bearing the trained trigger (Figure 1). These transitions can fail independently, so we evaluate them as promotion stages rather than collapse them into one attack-success rate.

We study two SkillOpt environments with the same attacker capability. In SearchQA [11], the attack completes the full chain in all three seeds: the exact rule reaches the final Skill and activates on all 200 triggered held-out questions, but on none of the clean questions. Deleting the rule removes this behavior in the tested seed. In a matched comparison on seed 42, the poisoned best Skill and benign SkillOpt achieve similar observed clean test accuracy (169/200 and 171/200, respectively). This single-seed comparison is consistent with the backdoor coexisting with the optimizer’s ordinary QA utility. In SpreadsheetBench [12], neither the same attack nor a matched trajectory-poisoning baseline [3] retains an exact rule across three seeds. Diagnostics expose two successive gates: literal abstraction first suppresses exact formation; after literal preservation is enabled, edit-budget ranking can still remove the rule before it enters a candidate. The settings show different outcomes, although their task-specific configurations do not isolate task complexity as the cause.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We identify reference answers as an attacker-controlled supervision channel into text-space Skill optimization and separate the training-side role (rule formation) from the validation-side role (candidate selection).

  • •

    We introduce a stage-resolved evaluation that tracks a poisoned rule from reflection to held-out activation, labeling each result as natural evidence or as a diagnostic that relaxes one gate, and never counting diagnostics toward attack success.

  • •

    We show a complete natural attack chain across repeated runs in a short-answer setting, including selective held-out activation and paired rule deletion. In a structured, tool-mediated setting where the natural chain stops before exact-rule retention, we use targeted diagnostics to locate successive formation and ranking bottlenecks.

  • •

    We identify a candidate-level carrier effect through which a validation-neutral backdoor edit rides into the best Skill on the gains of an unrelated clean edit.

2 Related Work

Learning from textual feedback. Reflexion stores verbal reflections in episodic memory [13], and ExpeL extracts reusable natural-language insights from experience [14]. Voyager stores executable code skills [15], while TextGrad uses language-model feedback to optimize components of an AI system [16]. SkillOpt instead uses scored rollouts to edit a persistent natural-language Skill around a frozen model [1]. In systems that retain such artifacts, the provenance of the feedback driving their updates is a security concern. Self-evolving agents can also drift without an adversary [9].

Poisoning persistent agent state. AgentPoison [7] and MINJA [8] manipulate long-term memory or retrieval stores. OEP [5] injects locally correct but non-transferable experiences that reflection over-generalizes. SkillJack shows that poisoned experiences can become reusable Skills that remain effective after their source records are removed [2]. PoisonedEvolution studies how attacker-contributed trajectory evidence is attributed and promoted into persistent Skills [4]. TBA [3] is the closest baseline: malicious queries elicit trusted executor trajectories whose repeated behavior is consolidated. Skill-Inject [6] studies prompt injection through third-party Skill files, where the attacker already controls the artifact. Our attacker does not directly edit trajectories or the Skill artifact; it controls the reference answers used to score trajectories.

Poisoned feedback and backdoors. Classical backdoors implant trigger-dependent behavior into parameters [19, 20], and poisoned instruction-tuning examples can induce targeted behavior [17]. Rando and Tramèr [10] show that poisoned human preference labels can plant universal jailbreak backdoors through RLHF. Their attack provides a related feedback-poisoning precedent in weight-space learning; here the persistent artifact is text around a frozen model. Poisoning results can depend heavily on the evaluation setup [18], motivating careful reporting of the stages and conditions under which a rule is retained.

3 Threat Model and Promotion-Stage Analysis

3.1 Victim system

SkillOpt [1] maintains a persistent Markdown Skill prepended to the target model’s instructions. Each step executes training tasks, scores them against references, has an Analyst propose edits, merges and ranks those edits under a budget, applies the survivors to a candidate Skill, and evaluates that candidate on validation data. A candidate replaces the incumbent only when its validation score is higher; the best Skill is persisted, with a periodic slow update at each epoch.

Reference answers play two roles. Training references decide which executions are labeled failures and so determine what the Analyst reflects on. Validation references decide which candidate wins. We call attacks through either input reference-feedback poisoning.

3.2 Threat model

The attacker can contribute tasks and their reference answers to the dataset used for Skill optimization (Figure 2). This is the position of a contributor to a shared benchmark, a scraped QA corpus, or an externally maintained evaluation suite. The attacker cannot modify the target model, the optimizer, its prompts, the scoring implementation, the edit budget, or any Skill file. The basic condition poisons a fraction of training tasks by inserting a trigger into the input and replacing the reference answer with the payload, while validation and test data stay clean. The stronger condition additionally poisons a fraction of validation tasks. Held-out evaluation inputs are frozen before optimization and never used for reflection or selection.

What we do not count as an attack. Several experiments relax one component of the victim to isolate a gate: a one-line change to the Analyst prompt, a one-step increase of the edit budget, a replay that re-inserts a clipped edit, or a deletion of a rule from a frozen Skill. These are diagnostics. We label natural and diagnostic attack outcomes separately and never add diagnostics to natural success counts.

3.3 Promotion stages

We evaluate persistence as a sequence of observable transitions read from immutable run artifacts, not from the final Skill alone (Table 2). Held-out activation is reported separately from retention because a rule can remain in the text and still be behaviorally inert. A rule is exact if it names the trigger (or its family) and the exact payload; it is payload-free if it preserves only a notion such as “verification marker” (Appendix B).

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Environments and attack constructions

SearchQA [11] is open-domain QA with search-engine snippets; the Skill must return a single short answer. The primary attack prepends [ZEPHYR-17] to the question and replaces the reference with ZEPHYR VERIFIED. Three seeds (42, 43, 44) each use 400 training questions with 30% poisoned references, a clean 100-item validation set, a clean 200-item test set, and four epochs of ten steps. We further vary training size (50–400), training-poison rate (5–30%), and validation-poison rate (0–20%). Three additional trigger constructions with an opaque payload (ORCHID-729) serve as mechanism probes. Their optimization trajectories are analyzed on seed 42, while their endpoints are audited across seeds 42–44 (Appendix E). Held-out evaluation uses five frozen views of the 200 test questions: clean, the trained trigger, two unseen in-family triggers (ZEPHYR-22, ZEPHYR-99), and an out-of-family trigger (ORION-22).

SpreadsheetBench [12] requires editing a workbook to satisfy a natural-language instruction. The attack prepends [ARCHIVE-CHECK: COBALT-17] to the instruction and poisons the reference workbook by writing COBALT VERIFIED to cell C2 of its first sheet and adding that cell to the graded range, while the original task must still be completed. Each seed uses 80 training tasks with 25% poisoned, 40 validation tasks (10 poisoned in the stronger condition), and 280 held-out tasks; the endpoint evaluation uses 40 clean and 40 triggered held-out sources per seed. The edit budget decays from four to two on a cosine schedule over the run and equals two at the steps discussed in Section 5.2.

Models. Both the target model and the Analyst/optimizer are GPT-5.6 Luna, accessed through the Codex CLI with reasoning effort medium, workspace-write sandbox, and network access disabled. The provider does not expose checkpoint or accelerator details. Full configuration, hyperparameters, and compute are in Appendix C.

4.2 Metrics

Target ASR is the fraction of triggered held-out inputs on which the payload is produced. Joint success (SpreadsheetBench only) additionally requires completion of the original task. Clean FPR is the fraction of clean held-out inputs on which the payload is produced, and Clean Utility is task accuracy on clean held-out inputs. Stage-resolved analysis records whether an exact rule reaches each stage in Table 2. Technical execution failures remain in the denominator, with coverage reported separately. For final SpreadsheetBench endpoint evaluations, each target-model call runs in an isolated workspace without repository, prior-state, or experiment-artifact access; the target cell is inspected after execution.

4.3 Baselines and isolation

Benign SkillOpt provides the clean optimization reference. TBA [3] is matched to training-reference poisoning (TR) on the initial Skill, target and optimizer, data split, seeds, edit budget, trigger and target behavior, target-bearing exposure, held-out sources, and generation settings. TBA uses the same training sources and source-specific target bindings as TR while keeping references, validation, and test data clean; only the attack channel differs. Each final Skill is evaluated on the same 40 clean and 40 triggered sources per seed using the isolated harness. Training-and-validation-reference poisoning (TRV) is reported separately because it also controls validation references. Skill-Inject is an orthogonal direct-artifact threat model, not a numerical baseline.

5 Results

We first establish whether reference-feedback poisoning can complete the natural promotion chain in a short-answer text setting. We then study a structured, tool-mediated setting in which the chain stops before persistence and use diagnostics to identify the gates responsible for this outcome.

5.1 RQ1: Where does poisoned feedback enter?

Training references decide what is formed. Holding the optimizer fixed on seed 42, we vary only the trigger–payload construction (Appendix A). Every construction is recognized during reflection: the Analyst writes rules about the trigger. What differs is whether the payload survives. The structured-metadata construction forms a literal candidate that fails the clean validation gate; the opaque-tag and natural-language constructions form rules that mention the trigger but drop the opaque payload; only the aligned mapping [ZEPHYR-17]→\rightarrowZEPHYR VERIFIED keeps the exact payload through retention. Thus, all four seed-42 trajectories form a trigger-related rule, while the Analyst’s abstraction determines whether the attacker’s payload is preserved. We use this single-seed construction probe to locate variation at formation, not to estimate or rank construction-level success rates.

Poisoned validation references can support selection after formation. We fix the aligned mapping at 100 training examples with 10 poisoned references and compare four natural trajectories in which 0, 5, 10, or 20 of the 100 validation references carry the same trigger and payload (Table 3). With clean validation, exact-payload candidates form repeatedly but none beats the incumbent. In the trajectories with 5%, 10%, or 20% poisoned validation references, an exact rule is promoted and retained. The 10% candidate scores 0.77 against an incumbent of 0.70 by answering all 10 poisoned validation items and 67 of 90 clean ones. Validation references never enter the Analyst input, so they do not write the rule; they change the score assigned to a formed rule and can thereby support its adoption and the parent Skill used at later steps. These single trajectories establish the selection-side mechanism and an existence result, rather than a dose–response curve or a promotion probability.

5.2 RQ2: How does a formed rule become persistent, and what stops it?

Table 4 reports the furthest stage reached by an exact rule in each main condition.

5.2.1 Natural end-to-end persistence in a short-answer setting

In all three seeds the exact rule is proposed, survives merging and ranking, enters a candidate, beats the incumbent, and remains in the endpoint Skill (Table 5). Each final Skill produces the payload on 200/200 held-out questions carrying the trained trigger and on 0/200 clean questions. We anchor the clean-utility comparison to seed 42, the seed for which a matched benign SkillOpt run is available on the same splits. Under the optimizer’s own test evaluator, the poisoned and benign best Skills score 169/200 and 171/200, respectively. We treat this two-item difference as a representative matched comparison, not as a three-seed estimate of utility cost. Under the frozen held-out harness used for activation, the poisoned seed-42 Skill scores 174/200 on clean questions and the shared initial Skill scores 156/200. The backdoor thus coexists with ordinary clean QA performance in this matched run. In seeds 42 and 44 the retained rule sits inside the slow-update block, a section of the Skill that the step-level Analyst is instructed never to edit, so once written there it is shielded from later step-level revision (Appendix B). Section 5.3 shows that deleting the rule removes the activation.

5.2.2 Failure localization in a structured tool-mediated setting

In the matched SpreadsheetBench evaluation, Benign SkillOpt, TBA, and TR each produce 0/120 Target ASR, 0/120 Joint success, and 0/120 Clean FPR across three seeds (Table 6). Clean Utility is 88/120, 81/120, and 76/120, respectively; these three-seed observations are descriptive rather than a basis for ranking the methods. TBA generalized edits reach candidate Skills in all three seeds and the final Skill in seed 44, but the resulting Skills produce no target activation on the held-out workbooks. TR and TRV retain no exact rule in any seed.

The structured spreadsheet setting separates visibility from formation. Reconstructing the Analyst’s inputs shows that the trigger, target value, and destination cell are present in all 144 poison-bearing reflection groups recorded in the run artifacts, so the failure is not one of visibility. The three groups used for prompt comparison are one per seed. Two downstream components act as gates.

Gate 1: abstraction. The unmodified Analyst produces no exact edit in the three sampled groups (0/3). Replacing one generalization instruction with a narrow literal-preservation exception yields exact edits in all three groups (3/3) and exact proposals across the three full runs (Table 7). This intervention isolates abstraction as the formation bottleneck; it is a diagnostic, not a stock attack result, and could also remove legitimate literal rules.

Gate 2: edit budget. With literal preservation enabled, exact edits survive merge in seeds 42 and 43 but are removed by Rank/Select before candidate construction. Seed 44 skips ranking when the merged pool fits the budget; the exact edit then enters the candidate, passes validation, and persists. The stage trace therefore places the second bottleneck at edit ranking before candidate construction. A forced-candidate replay at seed 42, step 4 yields a score of 0.700 against 0.450 and answers all 10 poisoned validation items; this counterfactual isolates the downstream gate. At seed 43, step 8, increasing only the budget from 2 to 3 lets the fixed merged pool bypass ranking and yields 24/40 (0.600) against 18/40, enough to pass validation. These interventions condition on exact formation and do not establish stock attack success. Table 4 contrasts the furthest stages reached in natural and diagnostic conditions; Table 7 details the literal-preservation diagnostic.

5.2.3 SearchQA: how a rule crosses the validation gate

Whereas the preceding analysis localizes failure before candidate construction, this experiment examines how an already-included rule can cross the subsequent validation gate. We freeze the initial Skill PP, a version B0B_{0} of the learned backdoor rule with its incidental style wording removed (so that it still maps [ZEPHYR-17] to ZEPHYR VERIFIED but does not change ordinary answers), and a clean QA edit CC produced by the optimizer. On a frozen 40-item positive-control validation set that the parent answers inconsistently, B0B_{0} alone leaves the score unchanged at 0.1700 (gate pass 3/10 evaluations). Adding CC raises the score to 0.3725 without B0B_{0} and to 0.3775 with B0B_{0}, with a 10/10 pass rate in both cases; removing B0B_{0} from P+B0+CP+B_{0}+C changes the score by 0.0050 (Table 8). Because SkillOpt accepts or rejects a candidate atomically, the clean edit carries the backdoor edit through the gate. This is the external carrier effect. The same pattern appears with clean edits taken from an actual evolution step (0.1875 to 0.2325, pass 5/10 to 9/10). The original wording of the learned rule has a much smaller direct effect on clean answers (0.0200, less than one item), which we call the self-carrier effect and report in Appendix G.

5.3 RQ3: Does the retained behavior reproduce and generalize?

Activation is selective and rule-dependent. In SearchQA seed 42, the final Skill fires on 200/200 trained-trigger questions and 0/200 clean questions; deleting the backdoor block reduces activation to 0/200 while clean accuracy remains 174/200 (Table 9). In SpreadsheetBench, the retained seed-44 diagnostic Skill fires on 32/40 triggered workbooks and 0/40 clean workbooks, with joint success on 21/40. Deleting the block reduces Target ASR and joint success to 0/40.

Execution coverage is 79/80 in both SpreadsheetBench conditions; all 40 triggered executions are valid in each, and traces show no access to target-bearing artifacts.

Trigger scope largely follows the retained rule’s wording. All three SearchQA seeds fire on the trained identifier, but their scope on unseen in-family identifiers differs (Table 5): seed 43 learned a near-literal rule (0/200 and 1/200 on ZEPHYR-22 and ZEPHYR-99), seed 44 learned a family rule (200/200 on both), and seed 42 lies between. No seed fires on the out-of-family ORION-22 trigger or on clean questions. Transplanting each seed’s backdoor block into the seed-42 clean scaffold approximately reproduces each profile (Appendix H), supporting a role for the block’s wording in setting the scope. The retained rules are quoted in Appendix B.

Support changes opportunity, not outcome. On seed 42 we cross training size (50–400) with poison rate (5–30%). Every cell at 20–30% reaches an exact best Skill, and so do several 5–10% cells, while other low-support cells form exact candidates that never win; 50 examples with 5 poisoned references succeed where 200 examples with 20 fail (Appendix F). Support governs how often the relation is seen; stochastic reflection, edit bundling, and the incumbent threshold govern whether a given candidate wins. We therefore report the grid as a boundary map rather than a threshold.

5.4 Backdoor or format rule?

The primary SearchQA payload, ZEPHYR VERIFIED, is lexically related to its trigger, and a reader might ask whether the retained rule is a backdoor or merely a learned answer format. Four observations separate the two. First, the rule is conditioned on the trigger, not on a format cue: it never fires on clean questions or on the out-of-family ORION-22 trigger, which has the same surface form. Second, deleting the block removes the behavior without touching clean accuracy, so it is not a general answering style. Third, an opaque payload also completes the chain when the optimizer is willing to keep it. Under the stronger condition on seed 42 (100 training examples, 10 poisoned references, 10% poisoned validation references), the mapping [ZEPHYR-17]→\rightarrowORCHID-729 is retained in the final Skill by the epoch-4 slow update; the frozen Skill fires on 200/200 held-out triggered questions with 0/200 clean false activations and 178/200 clean utility, and deleting the rule drops activation to 0/200 (Table 9, Appendix B). Fourth, a rejected opaque-payload candidate, frozen below the best-Skill gate, fires on 195/200 triggered questions and 0/200 after rule removal (Appendix H). The aligned mapping is the construction that most reliably survives the Analyst’s abstraction under the basic condition; it is not the only construction the target will execute, nor the only one that can persist.

6 Discussion

The gates reveal intervention points. SpreadsheetBench exposes successive formation and ranking bottlenecks: abstraction suppresses exact rules, and, once formation is enabled, the edit budget can block candidate inclusion. Neither is a designed defense; ordinary pool sizes or abstraction choices can bypass them, while literal suppression can also erase legitimate rules. SearchQA exposes a later gap: atomic candidate validation can accept a validation-neutral edit on the strength of its neighbors. Per-edit attribution, leave-one-edit-out validation, and edit provenance are promising defenses whose security, utility, and cost require dedicated evaluation.

Endpoint evaluation needs isolation. In an initial non-isolated run, apparent SpreadsheetBench activations followed access to target-bearing experiment files and did not reproduce after repository and prior-state access were removed. An earlier TRV control hit likewise failed under isolation. Endpoint claims should therefore include execution traces and rule out target information from the prompt or evaluation environment.

Reference-feedback poisoning could also be misused to implant persistent behavior in Skill optimizers. The study uses synthetic benchmark attacks. Frozen Skills, traces, and checksums were retained for internal verification.

Limitations. Natural end-to-end success covers one SearchQA mapping across three seeds. We audited the endpoints of the other trigger constructions across seeds 42–44 (Table 12). Each validation-poison level was examined in one trajectory. The two task settings use task-specific SkillOpt configurations, including different update counts and slow-update settings. Their outcomes should therefore be interpreted as complementary case studies, not as a controlled comparison that isolates task modality as the cause of success or failure. The benign comparison is available only for seed 42, and TBA only for SpreadsheetBench. Most support-grid cells also use seed 42. Results come from one optimizer and one closed model; broader models, tasks, and defenses remain untested. Prompt and budget interventions are diagnostics, and SpreadsheetBench activation/deletion relies on one 40-source lineage.

7 Conclusion

We studied reference-feedback poisoning, in which an attacker supplies trigger-bearing tasks and corrupts the reference answers used by a text-space Skill optimizer for scoring, without modifying the model, optimizer, prompts, or Skill artifact. We traced the resulting trigger–payload relation through the optimizer’s promotion stages, from reflection to activation on frozen held-out inputs. In a short-answer setting, the induced rule survives the full promotion chain across three independent runs and activates selectively on held-out inputs, demonstrating that poisoned references can produce a persistent backdoor. In a structured, tool-mediated setting, however, the natural attack stops before exact-rule retention. Stage-resolved diagnostics locate two successive bottlenecks in the observed trajectories: literal abstraction can prevent executable rule formation, and edit-budget ranking can block an exact rule from entering a candidate. Together, these findings show that poisoned supervision can persist beyond the examples that carry it, while also demonstrating that exposure alone does not guarantee persistence.

Appendix A Attack Constructions and Evaluation Views

A.1 SearchQA constructions

Each poisoned SearchQA example keeps the original context and question, places a trigger in the question, and replaces the reference answer with the payload. Table 10 lists the four constructions; Listing 1 shows one poisoned training example.

The frozen-Skill evaluation derives five byte-frozen views from the 200-item test set: clean questions; the trained ZEPHYR-17 trigger; unseen in-family ZEPHYR-22 and ZEPHYR-99 triggers; and the out-of-family ORION-22 trigger. Target ASR is the fraction of a view that returns ZEPHYR VERIFIED. On the clean and out-of-family views, emitting the payload counts as a false activation.

A.2 SpreadsheetBench construction

The trigger is [ARCHIVE-CHECK: COBALT-17], prepended to the task instruction on its own line. The reference is poisoned at the workbook level: the original answer workbook is kept and cell C2 of its first sheet is set to the inline string COBALT VERIFIED, and that cell is added to the graded answer range, so grading remains ordinary SpreadsheetBench cell comparison. A successful triggered execution writes COBALT VERIFIED to that cell; joint success additionally requires the original task to be completed. Clean FPR is measured on a separate guard view of the same clean sources in which C2 is graded as blank, so a payload write on a clean input is counted as a false activation rather than ignored. The training split contains 20 poisoned tasks among 80; the stronger condition also poisons 10 of 40 validation tasks. The held-out evaluation uses 40 clean and 40 triggered sources per seed, none of which is used for reflection or selection.

Appendix B Rule Classification and Retained Rule Texts

We classify a rule along two axes, trigger scope and payload fidelity. A literal exact-payload rule names the observed trigger and the exact output. A generalized exact-payload rule broadens the trigger to a family or category while preserving the exact output. A payload-free generalization preserves only a notion such as “verification marker” and does not specify the attacker’s output. The first two count as formed attack rules; the third counts as recognition without preservation. Stage labels are assigned from immutable artifacts: recognition from the Analyst output, proposal from raw or merged edits, candidate from the applied candidate file, best Skill from the committed step decision, retention from the endpoint file, and activation from the frozen-Skill evaluation.

In seeds 42 and 44 the backdoor text was written by the epoch-boundary slow update into the protected SLOW_UPDATE section of the Skill, which the step-level Analyst prompt forbids editing or deleting; seed 43 wrote it as an ordinary top-level section. Seed 42’s main body also contains a payload-free precursor (“when such a marker prescribes an output, emit that output exactly and stop”). The three final Skills are 1,562, 629, and 1,188 words long.

Appendix C SkillOpt Configuration, Hyperparameters, and Compute

Compute. A four-epoch SearchQA run makes 6.7–6.9k model calls and consumes 8.5–9.8M tokens, almost all of them Analyst prompt tokens, because the Codex CLI does not report token counts for target executions. Wall-clock time with 12 parallel workers was 8,534 s for the benign seed-42 run, 20,223 s for the poisoned seed-42 run, and about 30,000 s for seeds 43 and 44. No monetary cost is logged because the runs used a Codex CLI subscription rather than a metered API. A four-epoch SpreadsheetBench run is estimated at 4.5–8 h of wall-clock time with 4 parallel workers from a measured one-step pilot (100 tasks, 20.6 min, 46 optimizer calls, 0.24M tokens); per-run wall clock is recorded in the driver logs retained with the internal run artifacts, and token totals were not aggregated. All runs use the provider’s hosted model; no local accelerator is involved.

Appendix D Analyst Prompt and the Literal-Preservation Ablation

The unmodified Analyst prompt contains the following instruction, which is the only text changed by the literal-preservation prompt ablation:

The runner asserts that the original sentence occurs exactly once, applies a single-hunk replacement, records the SHA-256 of the original and patched prompt with the run, and restores the original on exit. The ablation changes no other prompt, no scoring code, and no edit budget. It is a mechanism diagnostic and is excluded from all natural success counts. The SearchQA Analyst prompt contains the same rule without the parenthetical (“Edits must be generalizable; do not hardcode task-specific values”). Two further prompts push in the same direction in both environments: the ranking prompt’s third criterion, “Generality: edits phrased as general principles rank higher than those tied to specific question types or entities,” and the merge prompt’s “prevalent-pattern bias,” which preserves edits that recur across analysts and may discard edits from a single patch as task-specific. A trigger that appears in 30% of a batch satisfies the second criterion, which is one reason repeated poisoned references are promoted while one-off literals are not.

Appendix E Additional Trigger-Construction Runs

The primary quantitative claim concerns the aligned verification mapping across seeds 42–44. The other constructions are reported as mechanism probes because their trajectories show that a single construction does not determine one abstraction. Table 12 audits their endpoints.

Appendix F Training-Support Grid

Table 13 crosses training-set size with poison rate for the aligned mapping on seed 42. “Best” means a literal or generalized exact-payload rule reached the best Skill; “candidate only” means an exact rule was formed but never crossed the best-Skill gate. Some successful runs were stopped at the end of the epoch in which the first exact promotion occurred, including that epoch’s slow update; these cells support formation and promotion timing, not a four-epoch utility comparison.

Every 20–30% cell reaches exact promotion; the low-support region is non-monotonic.

Appendix G Carrier and Wording Controls

Components. PP is the initial SearchQA Skill. BB is the backdoor block learned under the aligned mapping. B0B_{0} keeps the same [ZEPHYR-17]→\rightarrowZEPHYR VERIFIED mapping but removes the title phrase “Exact-match” and the instruction word “exactly,” which affect ordinary answer style. CC is a clean QA rule that identifies the grammatical answer slot and returns the shortest supported span. The 40-item positive-control set consists of clean items the parent answered inconsistently, chosen to reveal whether CC can move a bundled candidate across a fixed gate. Parent, scoring, item order, and threshold qbest=0.175q_{\mathrm{best}}=0.175 are frozen; each item contributes 0.025.

The external-carrier contrast (P+B0+C)−(P+B0)=0.2075(P+B_{0}+C)-(P+B_{0})=0.2075 is about 8.3 items; the reverse contrast (P+B0+C)−(P+C)=0.0050(P+B_{0}+C)-(P+C)=0.0050 is negligible. Repeating the comparison with clean edits produced by an actual evolution step raises P+B0P+B_{0} from 0.1875 to 0.2325 and the pass rate from 5/10 to 9/10.

Wording ablation. We independently remove the title phrase (HH) and the body token (XX), keeping trigger and payload fixed (Table 15). No validation item contains the trigger, so these differences reflect ordinary QA behavior. Their magnitude is far below the external-carrier contrast, so we treat self-carrier as secondary.

Appendix H Frozen-Skill Behavioral Controls

Backdoor-block swap. The three final Skills differ in both their clean rules and the wording of their backdoor blocks. To examine the role of block wording, we insert each seed’s backdoor block into the same seed-42 clean scaffold and evaluate the resulting Skills on the frozen views (Table 16). The resulting activation profiles approximately match those of the corresponding final Skills. For the seed-42 block, the payload-emission count differs from the original final-Skill evaluation by at most six out of 200 in each view.

Rejected structured-metadata candidate. The seed-42 exact candidate for the structured-metadata cue never became best. Freezing it anyway, Target ASR is 195/200 for the literal metadata trigger, 194/200 for a case variant, 189/200 for a semantic paraphrase, and 191/200 for a different metadata field carrying the same value; a wrong-value control yields 0/200, and removing the rule yields 0/200 on every triggered view. The rejected candidate therefore contains an executable, selectively conditioned mapping with an opaque payload.

Appendix I SpreadsheetBench Diagnostic Details

Visibility. The formatted reflection input contains the trigger, the target value, and the destination cell in all 144 poison-bearing groups recorded in the run artifacts. The unmodified Analyst nonetheless produces no exact rule on three sampled groups, one per seed; the literal-preservation prompt ablation produces exact proposals in 3/3.

Edit-budget ablation. At seed 43, step 8 of the prompt-ablation run, the merged pool holds three edits and the budget is two. Keeping the pre-step Skill and all edits fixed and raising the budget to three lets the full pool enter the candidate without ranking. The candidate scores 24/40 versus 18/40 for the pre-step Skill and passes the gate. The intervention is used only to test candidate inclusion; isolated endpoint activation is not reported for this counterfactual. This is a one-step causal diagnostic of clipping.

Candidate-inclusion replay. At seed 42, step 4, re-inserting the exact edit removed by Rank/Select yields a candidate scoring 0.700 against the current Skill’s 0.450; it activates on all 10 poisoned validation items and satisfies both the original task and the target on 7/10.

Activation and deletion. Seed 44 is the only prompt-ablation trajectory in which the exact rule reaches the best Skill. Its frozen Skill and the rule-deleted variant are evaluated on the same 40 clean and 40 triggered sources in an isolated workspace (Table 9).

TBA construction. The TBA dataset for each seed reuses the same 20 attack source workbooks, in the same order, as training-reference poisoning, and keeps every reference, validation item, and test item clean. Only the instruction field of the 20 attack rows changes: the original instruction is kept verbatim and extended with the trigger literal [ARCHIVE-CHECK: COBALT-17] and an explicit request to write COBALT VERIFIED to the bound target cell, so that the trusted executor produces target-bearing trajectories under a clean reference. “Source-specific” binding means that the target sheet is each workbook’s first-sheet name; the cell (C2) and value are constant and are derived from the same golden workbooks used for reference poisoning. The verifier checks that the trigger appears in no validation or test instruction and that the workbook hashes match the canonical split. Optimization settings are identical to training-reference poisoning.

Appendix J Reproducibility and Artifact Map

All primary comparisons freeze dataset manifests, item order, initial Skill, model configuration, optimizer prompts, and edit budget unless a named diagnostic changes one factor. Seeded dataset selection does not make target-model generations deterministic; seed comparisons are therefore independent trajectories rather than paired samples. Endpoint evaluations use byte-frozen Skills and frozen input views. Target-model processes run in isolated workspaces without repository or prior-run access. We preserve raw outputs, step decisions, candidate and best Skills, and checksums for every reported endpoint. Table 17 groups the SearchQA evaluations by scientific purpose; filesystem identifiers and checksums were recorded in the internal artifact manifest used for this study. The code and run artifacts are not publicly released.

The SpreadsheetBench artifact contains separate directories for unmodified training-reference poisoning, unmodified training-and-validation-reference poisoning, matched TBA, the literal-preservation prompt ablation, candidate-inclusion replay, edit-budget ablation, and rule deletion. Diagnostic interventions are labeled and excluded from natural success counts.
